Unit 1 of 10: Individual Differences and Psychological Attributes

Key ideas

  • Individual differences are the distinctiveness and variations among people's characteristics and behaviour patterns. Psychologists also study situationism — how situations shape behaviour.
  • Psychological attributes that are assessed: intelligence (global capacity to understand, think rationally and use resources effectively), aptitude (potential to acquire skills), interest (preference for activities), personality (characteristic ways of responding), values (beliefs about what is desirable).

Worked examples

Example 1: A student enjoys drawing but has not been trained. Which attribute is this? Answer: interest (and possibly aptitude if she shows potential).

10-mark practice set

  1. (1 mark, MCQ) The potential to acquire a skill with training is: (a) interest (b) aptitude (c) value (d) personality. Answer: (b).
  2. (1 mark) What is situationism? Answer: the view that situations and circumstances influence behaviour.
  3. (2 marks) Distinguish interest and aptitude. Answer: interest — preference for an activity (1); aptitude — potential to learn a skill (1).
  4. (3 marks) Name and define three psychological attributes. Answer: any three of intelligence, aptitude, interest, personality, values — correctly defined (1 each).
  5. (3 marks) Why is it important to study individual differences? Answer: helps in career and educational guidance (1); identifies special needs (1); explains why people respond differently to the same situation (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Aptitude and achievement confused. 2. Values called interests. 3. No definitions. 4. Situationism missed. 5. No applications.

Quick recall

  1. Potential for skill? 2. Preferences? 3. Desirable beliefs? 4. Characteristic responses? 5. Situational influence?

Answers: 1) Aptitude. 2) Interest. 3) Values. 4) Personality. 5) Situationism.
